📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, you've got everything ready - data, model, a beefy GPU setup. You hit "run" and... wait. And wait some more. Your GPUs are barely breaking a sweat while your wallet's getting lighter by the hour.

Sound familiar? We've been there. After some detective work on our nanoVLM project, we discovered the real culprit wasn't our model or hardware, it was our data pipeline being incredibly wasteful.

In this post we build an efficient pipeline in five stages. In each stage we add or remove from the previous step and comment on what went right and what did not.

Industry observers note that to make it easier to follow the data preparation tasks, we created a separate repo laser-focused on the data pipeline only. We hope this will be much easier to understand that reading the code once integrated with the nanoVLM repository. In addition, this could be useful to bootstrap other data pipelines!

Repository: https://github.com/ariG23498/mmdp.

To follow along, all you need to do is clone the repository. It contains the final data preparation tasks, but it's designed to showcase each step of the way.

Before optimizing anything, we need to understand what we are working with. Our multimodal dataset has images, text prompts, and responses.

Getting familiar with your training data is crucial for success. The previous script shows a random sample each time you run it; you may want to copy the snippet to a notebook and run it multiple times to get a feeling about the data.

Our first training attempt used the obvious (and very frequent) approach:.

It has been revealed that the results were painful. Look at this visualization:.

See all that gray? That's padding. That's the GPU processing absolutely nothing while you pay for compute time. We were wasting roughly 60% of our batch on empty tokens.

In a recent development, our next move was simple. Set a global maximum length and stick to it. If a sample was too long, we'd just drop it.

It has been revealed that as you might have noticed that the batch now has one sample less. This is due to the filtering process. This helped, but we were still padding everything to the same fixed length regardless of actual content. Better than before, but still wasteful.

Recent findings suggest that now we’re ready to rethink batching entirely. Padding is the enemy, and we need a strategy to minimize it while maximizing how much data we can fit into each batch. Enter the knapsack problem, a classic from computer science that’s perfect for this.

In a recent development, imagine you’re packing a backpack for a hike. It can only hold so much weight, and you want to cram in as many useful items as possible. In our case:.

To test this idea, we start with a toy dataset: just a list of numbers from 1 to 25, each representing a sequence length. This lets us experiment without the complexity of images and text.

Sources indicate that most PyTorch datasets are map-style (you access them with dataset[i]). But for dynamic batching, we need something more flexible. So, we built an iterable-style dataset by subclassing torch.utils.data.IterableDataset. This lets us generate batches on the fly and handle tricks like sharding data across multiple workers:.

It has been revealed that packing sequences can be slow, especially if we’re sorting or shuffling. To keep things moving, we use a producer-consumer pattern using Python queues:.

In a recent development, the producer thread packs batches and puts them in a queue, while the main thread pulls them out as needed. This overlap keeps the pipeline flowing smoothly.

First, we try a simple greedy packing strategy:.

Recent findings suggest that this walks through the data sequentially, adding items to a pack until it’s full, then starting a newly introduced one. It’s fast but not perfect. Here’s what the batches look like:.

It has been revealed that notice how later batches get sparse? We’re leaving gaps.

Let’s try a smarter approach: bin-packing (specifically, First Fit Decreasing):.

Industry observers note that this sorts sequences by length (longest first) and tries to fit each one into the first pack that has room. If none fits, it starts a new pack. The result?

These batches are much tighter, with less wasted space. It’s like playing Tetris with your data, fitting pieces together snugly.

Now for the real deal, applying knapsack packing to our multimodal dataset.

It has been revealed that we’re back to images, prompts, and responses, and we need to pack them efficiently while respecting both token limits and image budgets. Image budgeting is done so that images per sample are balanced. We would like to avoid the case where one GPU needs to process way more images than another.

Our new ConstantLengthDataset class handles the heavy lifting. Here’s how it works, compared to Stage 4:.

The ConstantLengthDataset does it all:.

Sources indicate that look at that! The gray (padding) is minimal, and the batches are dense with useful data. It’s like packing a suitcase so well you can still zip it up without sitting on it.

The image might seem unintuive at the first glance, but let us look at the image side by side with constrained padding.

In a recent development, here you will notice that the samples in knapsack are more evenly distributed. We also do not run into the glitch of having less samples in the batch due to filtering.

What started as a simple "why is training so slow?" investigation led to a complete rethink of how we handle multimodal data.

The balanced knapsack strategy for data pipeline comes from the Eagle 2: Building Post-Training Data Strategies from Scratch for Frontier Vision-Language Models paper from NVIDIA.

Happy training (and may your GPUs stay busy)!

A suspected poacher has reportedly been electrocuted to death by a trap intended to kill wild animals, while police are searching for two men who accompanied him on a hunting trip.

The incident occurred in India, near Bhitarkanika National Park, where farmers have reportedly been using illegal traps to kill wild animals that damage their crops.

According to the reports, the deceased was identified as a resident of Bhopal village named Nayak.

His wife, Sabitri, filed a police complaint alleging that villagers had taken her husband out to hunt wild boars at around 7 PM on November 24.

When he failed to return home, his family began searching for him. Local residents discovered his body in an agricultural field the following morning.

According to Ommcom News, Nayak had burn injuries on his hands, while a flashlight, stick, and wire were recovered at the scene.

Subsequent reports suggest Nayak had set the deadly trap himself, but instead the animals stayed clear from it.

The farmer reportedly intended to kill wild boars and spotted deer but forgot to disconnect the electricity before returning to his field to harvest crops, accidentally electrocuting himself.

In a recent development, police have opened an investigation and sent his body to a hospital for an autopsy. The whereabouts of his two alleged hunting companions remain unknown.

The incident comes just two months after another suspected poacher was reportedly trampled to death by elephants after illegally entering South Africa’s Kruger National Park.

Earlier in 2026, a California millionaire was killed by five elephants during a licensed hunting expedition in Gabon.

#218369. Queen's Domain review

Queen's Domain review

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2365 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Eurogamer

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that where to start with Queen's Domain?
  • It has been revealed that all this begins with an island.
  • Sources indicate that there is so much to say about Neasied.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that where to start with Queen's Domain? It's tempting to begin with King's Field; after all, FromSoftware's seminal first-person action-RPG is an explicit inspiration for developer Freshly Baked Games. But 40 hours later, it feels like so much more. It's equally tempting to invoke another FromSoftware game: Dark Souls. Queen's Domain owes an obvious debt to that game's celebrated level design: the dazzling interconnectedness of its vertiginous world. But that's not quite right either. The deeper you delve, the more there's something of the spirit of The Legend of Zelda, a touch of Metroidvania too. Until finally you concede that Queen's Domain, with its remarkable world of densely packed secrets, is very much its own.

It has been revealed that all this begins with an island. You, Prince Beruim, are a castaway, washed ashore on Neasied. Your father, the king, has disappeared, and your search has brought you, somewhat circuitously, here. As you clamber to your feet and survey the island, it makes an immediately striking impression: all strange peaks and crooked spires; a cramped, chaotic mass of landmarks lost amid the dense undergrowth. Pyramids perch atop steep plateaus; a vast, moss-tinged mausoleum sprawls across the land to one side while the other is dominated by an imposing tower. It's a world made all the stranger by Queen's Domain's retro aesthetic. Here, shimmering low-res textures and low-poly shapes converge to create elaborate spaces and structures that feel slightly at odds with the lo-fi vibe. It's not quite old, not quite upcoming; instead, something of a world lost outside of time. It makes for an enigmatic, disorientating landscape. And when paired with a soundtrack that delights in discordance, as it swings from gentle ambience to pulsing synths, it's a mood that refuses to resolve.

Sources indicate that there is so much to say about Neasied. And so much I absolutely will not spoil. But very early impressions don't do it justice at all. As you take your first tentative steps onto the island, presented with a forking path that eventually winds back in on itself, it's easy to mistake Queen's Domain for a first-person Dark Souls - especially if, like me, you're only passingly familiar with King's Field. As in most Soulslikes, early progress is defined by a punishing inch-by-inch crawl from one brutal encounter to the next; where death - via chicken-cricket hybrids, ladybird-rats, and other wonderfully odd things - comes fast and frequently, respawning you back at the last Crystal Monument you visited. And because its wilfully old-school design eschews modern-day niceties such as a combat lock-on or dedicated roll button, there's a looseness to fighting that takes a while to click. But it does, slowly, click.

Recent findings suggest that this is a game that demands you lean into its limitations, encourages you to find ways to make them work. At first, those Souls-honed instincts are likely to be your undoing as you naturally scramble for a dodge button that isn't there. But soon a different sort of pattern emerges: you realise that to avoid a ladybird attack, you simply need to step back - but not so far you don't have time to nip in and strike while your opponent takes a pause. A charging enemy might require a different approach - a well-timed backstep and swivelling sideways strafe to put you in the right place for a counter. And in this way, combat becomes a compelling sort of puzzle as you learn each of the 100+ enemies' little ticks - including rock, paper, scissors-style weaknesses to different weapon types - and figure out how to respond.

There's more to consider. Your melee damage output, for instance, is directly tied to your stamina bar: the more stamina you have, the harder you'll hit; too low and it's a waste of a swing. That forces you to choose your moments carefully, moving out to safety while your bar refills. And there's a charge attack, also linked to your stamina, that does more damage still. Already combat has a distinctively deliberate rhythm, but then come your first throwing knives. These are most immediately useful against enemies ordinarily out of reach - like the laser-spewing foliage dogging your journey early on - but they're equally valuable for luring individual enemies away from the throng. Throwing weapons take a while to return to your pouch, meaning they too need to be deployed with purpose. And while knives are just the start - you'll acquire an increasingly exotic selection of throwables including poison-tipped darts and homing blades - they all fundamentally work the same way.

It has been revealed that and the interplay of these various warm-ups and cooldowns creates an increasingly engaging rhythm as you learn to juggle between your variously equipped weapons to maximise their damage potential. You might, for instance, fire off a one-two-three volley of homing darts, then use a magic lantern to toss out a massive fireball that bounces destructively around the room. And it's there, in the ensuing chaos, you'll charge up your blade, letting rip then returning to your darts again. Combat might encourage a methodical pace, but that doesn't mean you can't fight fast, and there are some fascinating synergies among the various weapons, many having their own wonderfully distinct mechanisms. There's a brawling gauntlet that lifts you clean off the ground and a vampiric blade capable of stealing an enemy's life force. There are hammers, creatures, and an unexpected mid-game weapon class, utilising a third rechargeable power source, that I am definitely not spoiling. Queen's Domain's 100 or so weapons create ample space for experimentation and customisation, and the further from its cautious beginnings you stray, the brisker, the more exhilarating its combat becomes. In my current, late-game form, I'm a whirl of blades and blasts and up-close attacks that feels anything but Soulslike.

Industry observers note that queen's Domain isn't just a nippier sort of game, though. It quickly reveals itself to be friendlier, more accommodating. Levelling, for instance, happens passively as you play, meaning every swing feels like it's contributing to your progress. Weapons level independently too, encouraging specialisation. There are no flasks, no accumulated currency you'll need to worry about dropping on death, no subsequent corpse runs. And progress can be saved at any time using the nearest Crystal Monument, meaning that when you respawn, you won't have to grind through the same opponents again. Enemies do eventually reappear of their own accord, so you can't exploit the save system indefinitely. But unlike Souls-style bonfires, Crystal Monuments only repopulate the world when you explicitly tell them to - when you Rest to clear status effects and restore health - giving you considerably more agency. You can decide when to push forward, when to retreat and lock in your progress, and when to reap the benefits of a rest and reset. Together, it makes for a breezier, less punishing, more consistently rewarding riff on the traditional Souslike, while never losing that I-can-do-this just-one-more-turn allure.

According to recent reports, but as immensely enjoyable as Queen's Domain's combat is, the real draw here, unquestionably, is the world. Neasied is extraordinary. Right from the start, as you pick yourself off the sand and survey the landscape, its enigmatic huddle of peculiar landmarks isn't just intriguing, it's inviting. These odd pyramids, these curious plateaus practically demand to be explored. But how? The answer comes perhaps an hour in when, fancily clad skeleton boss successfully slain, you get your hands on the Holy Sword Endu. It's an immediate boon, far more lethal than the rubbish rusty blade you've been wielding so far. And its secondary attack - a long-range jab that propels you forward - is handy too. It's also your key to unlocking Neasied.

Endu's violent forward momentum can, you see, fling you across previously uncrossable gaps, gradually carrying you further and further as more upgrades reveal themselves. Suddenly, Queen's Domain takes flight, quite literally, becoming something closer to an exploratory sandbox as it adopts the spirited acrobatics of a platform game. And as you experiment with your newfound freedom, the more paths you explore, the island begins to take on a dizzying newly introduced form. Neasied, when viewed from up high, reveals itself to be a vastly intricate traversal puzzle. That peculiar structure in the distance? If you can find an appropriate ledge to fling yourself from, it's now yours for the investigating - and from there, one, two, three more tantalising branches are revealed. Neasied is an astonishing piece of design: a ludicrous, elaborate tangle of hidden pathways and secrets, forever folding in and around itself, that's crafted to invite curiosity and then constantly reward.

It has been revealed that freshly Baked Games always feels one step ahead. I can't recall a single moment where my exploratory What-ifs - What if I throw myself this way? What if I do a falling mid-air turn? What if I toss myself down this hole? - didn't bear fruit. Sometimes your prize is a steaming platter of boon-granting food, sometimes it's another bit of increasingly exotic weaponry. Perhaps you'll find a strange NPC with a favour to ask; fish eggs and mysterious skulls; a shopkeeper with a thing for ducks (who, in a typically lovely touch, festoons his store with the goods you're willing to sell), and so many mysterious upcoming puzzle threads to pull. As you fling and probe and push on forward, that thing you've been carrying around for hours - or, conversely, that thing you saw hours ago - suddenly finds new purpose. There's a definite touch of Metroidvania as old areas reveal new truths the further you go. And because there's so little handholding, so little explicit direction, every discovery feels like your own.

Recent findings suggest that but just as you think you're starting to get a handle on Queen's Domain's shape, along comes another surprise: dungeons as vastly intricate as the world outside. You'll navigate labyrinthine waterlogged caverns of angry fish where progress involves puzzling past ancient mechanisms. Later, an arcane tower where gargoyles prowl. Here, the convoluted upward route takes circuitous laps among the endless bookshelves, spilling out the windows onto teetering precipices with alarming sea views. Then down, however briefly, to eerie chambers below. Suddenly, the mood is less Soulslike, more Zelda, and your expectations shift again. And still upcoming discoveries lead to new paths and fresh mysteries.

Sources indicate that and it keeps on going. As Freshly Baked Games gradually peels back Neasied's layers, it constantly finds new ways to awe: yet more surprises, yet more secrets, your exploratory digressions earning still more intriguing rewards. There comes a point where you think surely you must have seen everything, explored its deepest caverns and most mysterious tombs, but down you go again. And somewhere around the midpoint, Queen's Domain takes a truly audacious turn. There is a - let's call it a tonal lurch for fear of spoilers - that signals another shift. Suddenly, there are new toys to play with, an autumnal landscape so complex in its demands, it genuinely made my brain pulse. And then it's over. Until it's not.

There are, it turns out, secrets beneath the secrets; a still more intricate web of interconnected threads spun throughout this already fascinating, impossibly complex world. The Neasied that welcomes you really is just the tip of it all. Exactly when you'll come to this realisation depends how thorough you are in the earlier hours - how willing you are to explore its darker corners and brave its more punishing realms - but for me the before-and-after managed to divide my 40-ish hour playthrough neatly in two. You reawaken with a sense of a quest unfulfilled, a hint that more is required. And so, in lieu of more explicit direction, you set out again, probe deeper, explore further, and slowly the vaguest shape of a new objective - a succession of tiny threads seemingly all leading in the same direction - begins to emerge. Tucked along uncharted paths, perhaps, or in suspicious corners, or in item descriptions that suddenly feels like clues.

It's here in this second half - something of a dark mirror to the first, in classic Zelda style - that Queen's Domain takes on a more esoteric air; its web of distantly scattered enigmas requiring real dedication to unfurl. Why this pot on a stick? Why this book? How do these unlit lanterns relate to this thing, and that thing, and this other thing on the other side of the world?

It's clever stuff, even if navigating its late-game threads can occasionally feel just a little too much, a little too abstruse, and you'll potentially face a lot of needle-in-a-haystack backtracking if you haven't been taking judicious notes as you go. Do I have any other quibbles? There are perhaps too few boss encounters that feel like genuine events. And while combat generally feels fair and balanced, serving as a propulsive drumbeat to the broader exploratory rhythms, there are a few late-game all-the-enemies-at-once-style difficulty spikes that go just a bit too far. But then another 'What if?' and the world responds, and those frustrations melt away.

I remember a time in my youth - back before dataminers and FAQs - when video games felt unknowable. Endless enigmas built from creativity and code. It felt like anything could be hiding in there if only you knew where to look, and it was easy to let your imagination run wild. Queen's Domain is so full of secrets, so full of mystery and wonder, it feels like the sort of game my enthusiastic child-brain might have dreamed up all those years ago. 40 hours in, I've seen an ending, but it feels like I'm still far from through. So many mysteries still linger, so many things remain on my checklist of speculative to-dos. Out in the real-world, I've got a Zelda and a GTA awaiting. But it says everything about Queen's Domain - this brilliant, vast, deep enigma; this absurdly audacious thing - that I'm still not yet ready to let go.

A copy of Queen's Domain was provided for this review by Future Friends Games.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that artificial intelligence could help overcome one of the biggest challenges in restoring vision to people who are blind: getting a brain implant to produce reliable visual experiences. Researchers from three institutions, including UC Santa Barbara, have demonstrated that AI can improve how precisely an experimental visual prosthesis stimulates the brain and predicts what a person perceives.

The team used a deep learning system to develop electrical stimulation patterns for electrodes temporarily implanted in the visual cortex, the region at the back of the brain responsible for processing visual information. By analyzing the brain's responses, the technology gave researchers greater control over neural activity and helped them better anticipate the visual sensations produced by the implant.

It has been revealed that published online in the journal Neuron, the proof-of-concept study represents progress toward more advanced visual prostheses, sometimes described as bionic eyes. These devices could eventually become more effective by learning how each person's brain responds to stimulation rather than relying on predetermined settings.

"Building a model in the abstract is one thing," noted Michael Beyeler, an associate professor of computer science and psychological and brain sciences at UC Santa Barbara. "Seeing it shape an experiment with a person is something else entirely. That ability to go from theory to something that may one day help people is what drives much of the work in our lab.".

How Bionic Vision Could Bypass Damaged Eyes.

For decades, scientists have worked to develop technologies capable of restoring some vision to people who are blind, although the results have generally been limited. Some experimental devices stimulate the retina, the layer of tissue at the back of the eye that detects light. Others attempt to activate parts of the visual system farther along the pathway that carries visual information to the brain.

Industry observers note that visual cortical prostheses work differently. Instead of depending on the eyes or optic nerves, they deliver electrical signals directly to the visual cortex. This approach could offer a potential solution for people whose visual pathways have been damaged but whose visual cortex can still respond to stimulation. Possible candidates include individuals who lost their sight because of strokes, neurodegenerative diseases, or traumatic brain injuries.

The ability to regain even limited vision could be especially meaningful for people who remember what it was like to see.

Beyeler highlighted those "who have been able to see for part of their life, but then, because of an inherited eye disease or an accident, have lost their vision," adding, "For those people, the desire may be very strong to get some vision back.".

Recent findings suggest that the newly introduced findings build on earlier computational research supported by Beyeler's 2022 National Institutes of Health (NIH) Director's New Innovator Award. The five-year, $2 million grant has supported his efforts to make artificial vision systems more accurate, predictable, and effective.

Scientists Test AI With a Brain Implant in a Blind Man.

An important opportunity to test the technology came in 2024, when researchers from Beyeler's Bionic Vision Lab traveled to Spain. Their goal was to determine whether their computer models could improve the performance of a brain implant already being used in an experimental study.

Sources indicate that at Hospital IMED Elche, the team worked with a 27-year-old man who had become blind following a traumatic brain injury. He had received an implant containing 96 electrodes arranged in an array within his visual cortex. The device was intended to remain in place for six months before being removed.

It has been revealed that when researchers activated the electrodes using electrical current, the participant experienced visual sensations known as phosphenes. These can appear as spots, flashes, or shapes of light, sometimes resembling stars or fireworks.

Producing these sensations is possible, but making them consistent and predictable is much more difficult. The same electrical stimulation does not always trigger an identical response, and activating particular electrodes does not guarantee that the person will perceive a specific visual pattern.

To address this problem, the researchers trained a deep neural network, a type of AI designed to recognize complex patterns, to predict how the visual cortex would respond to different electrical stimulation settings. The model also considered the brain's resting activity immediately before stimulation, giving it information about the participant's current neural state.

Using these predictions, the researchers identified combinations of electrical signals that were most likely to produce particular patterns of brain activity.

AI Makes Bionic Vision More Precise.

Industry observers note that when the scientists tested the stimulation patterns selected by AI, the results were encouraging. The new approach generated the intended patterns of neural activity more accurately than the comparison methods while requiring less electrical current.

Another important discovery emerged when the team examined the relationship between brain activity and the participant's visual experiences. The patterns recorded directly from his brain were better predictors of what he perceived than the stimulation settings themselves.

This distinction matters because activating the brain is not the same as knowing what a person will see. Even when researchers can produce a desired neural response, they still need to understand how the brain transforms that activity into a conscious visual experience.

"Engineers naturally want to treat phosphenes like pixels: stimulate more electrodes, and you should get a more complete image," Beyeler stated. "But the brain does not work that way. Electrodes interact, neural responses fluctuate, and what we put into the brain is not necessarily what the person perceives. The challenge is to learn more about that transformation.".

Industry observers note that the findings suggest that future visual prostheses may need to do more than simply deliver electrical signals. They may also need to monitor how the brain reacts and use that feedback to continually improve stimulation.

Teaching Brain Implants to Adapt to Each Person.

Recent findings suggest that A key advantage of the implant used in the experiment was its ability to perform two tasks. It could stimulate the visual cortex with electrical current while simultaneously recording the resulting neural activity.

This allowed researchers to train their AI model using the brain's actual responses rather than relying exclusively on information about which electrodes were activated and how much current they delivered.

The participant also provided feedback about what he experienced. He reported whether he saw a phosphene and, during certain experiments, described its appearance, including its shape, size, brightness, and color.

Comparing these reports with the recorded brain activity revealed that neural responses contained more useful information about the perceived visual sensations than the electrical stimulation parameters alone.

It has been revealed that the AI system also used measurements of resting brain activity to account for changes in the participant's neural state before each stimulation. This could be particularly valuable because the brain's response to electrical signals can vary over time, including from one day to the next.

By adapting stimulation to these changing conditions, future prostheses might provide more consistent visual experiences without requiring owners to adjust to a rigid set of signals.

According to recent reports, "A useful visual prosthesis cannot rely on a fixed recipe," Beyeler noted. "It has to learn how an individual brain responds and adapt the stimulation accordingly. Ultimately, the device should adapt to the person, not the other way around.".

A Collaborative Step Toward Restoring Sight.

Recent findings suggest that the research brought together scientists from UC Santa Barbara, ETH Zurich, and Miguel Hernández University (MHU). Beyeler described the effort as "a true collaboration.".

Industry observers note that the project was led by co-first authors Pehuén Moure of ETH Zurich, Jacob Granley of UC Santa Barbara, and Fabrizio Grani of MHU. The supervising researchers were Beyeler, Shih-Chii Liu of ETH Zurich, and Eduardo Fernández of MHU. Their work forms part of a larger feasibility trial taking place in Spain.

Although the technology remains experimental and the participant's visual experiences were limited to flashes and shapes of light, the results demonstrate how AI could improve communication between artificial vision devices and the brain.

Rather than treating every brain as if it responds the same way, future bionic vision systems could learn from each individual and adjust their signals accordingly. That personalized approach may prove essential to developing implants that can eventually restore useful vision to people who have lost their sight.

Three Mighty Alerts Supporting Hugging Face’s Production Infrastructure

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, the Infrastructure team at Hugging Face is excited to share a behind-the-scenes look at the inner workings of Hugging Face's production infrastructure, which we’ve had the privilege of helping to build and maintain.
  • In this blog post, we’ll dive into the details of three mighty alerts that play their unique role in supporting our production infrastructure, and explore how they've helped us maintain the high level of performance and uptime that our community relies on.
  • Oftentimes, with cloud computing architectures, where data flows between private and public networks, implementing a NAT (Network Address Translation) gateway stands as a steadfast best practice.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, the Infrastructure team at Hugging Face is excited to share a behind-the-scenes look at the inner workings of Hugging Face's production infrastructure, which we’ve had the privilege of helping to build and maintain. Our team's dedication to designing and implementing a robust monitoring and alerting system has been instrumental in ensuring the stability and scalability of our platforms. We’re constantly reminded of the impact that our alerts have on our ability to identify and respond to potential challenges before they become major incidents.

In this blog post, we’ll dive into the details of three mighty alerts that play their unique role in supporting our production infrastructure, and explore how they've helped us maintain the high level of performance and uptime that our community relies on.

Oftentimes, with cloud computing architectures, where data flows between private and public networks, implementing a NAT (Network Address Translation) gateway stands as a steadfast best practice. This gateway acts as a strategic gatekeeper, monitoring and facilitating all outbound traffic towards the public Internet. By centralizing egress traffic, the NAT gateway offers a strategic vantage point for comprehensive visibility. Our team can easily query and analyze this traffic, making it an invaluable asset when working through security, cost optimization or various other investigative scenarios.

Cost optimization is a critical aspect of cloud infrastructure management, and understanding the pricing dynamics is key. In data centers, pricing structures often differentiate between east-west traffic (typically communication within the same rack or building) and north-south traffic (communication between further away private networks or the internet). By monitoring network traffic volume, Hugging Face gains valuable insights into these traffic patterns. This awareness allows us to make informed decisions regarding infrastructure configuration and architecture, ensuring we limit incurring needless costs.

Industry observers note that one of our key alerts is designed to notify us when our network traffic volume surpasses a predefined threshold. This alert serves multiple purposes. Firstly, it acts as an early warning system, alerting us to any unusual spikes in traffic that might indicate potential challenges or unexpected behavior. Secondly, it prompts us to regularly review our traffic trends, ensuring we stay on top of our infrastructure's growth and evolving needs. This alert is set at a static threshold, which we have fine-tuned over time, ensuring it remains relevant and effective. When triggered, it often coincides with periods of refactoring our infrastructure.

For instance, when integrating third-party security and autoscaling tools, we've observed increased telemetry data egress from our nodes, triggering the alert and prompting us to optimize our configurations.

On another occasion, adjustments to our infrastructure lead to mistakenly avoiding a private, low-cost path between product-specific infrastructure (ex. traffic destined to the Hub from a Space to interact with repository data). To elaborate further, the most impactful workloads in terms of cost savings we’ve found are those that access object storage. Fetching objects directly prices cheaper than going through CDN-hosted assets for our LFS repository storage and additionally does not require the same security measures that our WAF provides compared to public requests arriving at our front door. Leveraging DNS overrides to switch traffic through private network paths and public network paths has become a valuable technique for us, driven by the CDKTF AWS provider.

As a final note, while we have configuration-as-code ensuring the desired state is always in effect, having an additional layer of alerting around helps in case mistakes are made when expressing the desired state through code.

The logging infrastructure at Hugging Face is a sophisticated system designed to collect, process, and store vast amounts of log data generated by our applications and services. At the heart of this system is the Hub application logging pipeline, a well-architected solution that ensures Hub model usage data is efficiently captured, enriched, and stored for reporting and archival purposes. The pipeline begins with Filebeat, a lightweight log shipper that runs as a daemonset alongside our application pods in each Kubernetes cluster. Filebeat's role is to collect logs from various sources, including application containers, and forward them to the next stage of the pipeline.

Once logs are collected by Filebeat, they are sent to Logstash, a powerful log processing tool. Logstash acts as the data processing workhorse, applying a series of mutations and transformations to the incoming logs. This includes enriching logs with GeoIP data for geolocation insights, routing logs to specific Elasticsearch indexes based on predefined criteria, and manipulating log fields by adding, removing, or reformatting them to ensure consistency and ease of analysis. After Logstash has processed the logs, they are forwarded to an Elasticsearch cluster.

Recent findings suggest that elasticsearch, a distributed search and analytics engine, forms the core of our log storage and analysis platform. It receives the logs from Logstash and applies its own set of processing rules through Elasticsearch pipelines. These pipelines perform minimal processing tasks, such as adding timestamp fields to indicate the time of processing, which is crucial for log analysis and correlation. Elasticsearch provides a scalable and flexible storage solution, allowing us to buffer logs for operational use and real-time analysis.

Industry observers note that to manage the lifecycle of logs within Elasticsearch, we employ a robust storage and lifecycle management strategy. This ensures that logs are retained in Elasticsearch for a defined period, providing quick access for operational and troubleshooting purposes. After this retention period, logs are offloaded to long-term archival storage. The archival process involves an automated tool that reads logs from Elasticsearch indexes, formats them as Parquet files—an efficient columnar storage format—and writes them to our object storage system.

The final stage of our logging pipeline leverages AWS data warehousing services. Here, AWS Glue crawlers are utilized to discover and classify data in our object storage, automatically generating a Glue Data Catalog, which provides a unified metadata repository. The Glue table schema is periodically refreshed to ensure it remains up-to-date with the evolving structure of our log data. This integration with AWS Glue enables us to query the archived logs using Amazon Athena, a serverless interactive query service. Athena allows us to run SQL queries directly against the data in object storage, providing a cost-effective and scalable solution for log analysis and historical data exploration.

Another point of fragility is the auto-schema detection mechanism in Elasticsearch. While it is designed to adapt to changing log structures, it can fail when application logs undergo significant field type changes. If the schema detection fails to recognize the newly introduced field types, it may lead to failed writes from Logstash to Elasticsearch, causing log processing bottlenecks and potential data inconsistencies. This issue highlights the importance of proactive log schema management and the need for robust monitoring to detect and address such issues promptly.

Industry observers note that memory management is also a critical aspect of the pipeline's stability. The log processing tier, including Logstash and Filebeat, operates with limited memory resources to control costs. When backpressure occurs, these components can experience Out-of-Memory (OOM) issues, especially during system slowdowns. As logs accumulate and backpressure increases, the memory footprint of these processes grows, pushing them closer to their limits. If not addressed promptly, this can lead to process crashes or further exacerbation of the backpressure problem.

Archival jobs, responsible for transferring logs from Elasticsearch to object storage, have also encountered challenges. On occasion, these jobs can be resource-intensive, with their performance becoming sensitive to node size and memory availability. In cases where junk data or unusually large log entries pass through the pipeline, they can strain the archival process, leading to failures due to memory exhaustion or node capacity limits. This underscores the importance of data validation and filtering earlier in the pipeline to prevent such issues from reaching the archival stage.

Recent findings suggest that to mitigate these potential failures, we've implemented a powerful alert system with a unique motivation: validating end-to-end log flow. The alert is designed to compare the number of requests received by our Application Load Balancer (ALB) with the number of logs successfully archived, providing a comprehensive view of log data flow throughout the entire pipeline. This approach allows us to promptly identify any discrepancies that might indicate potential log loss or processing issues.

According to recent reports, the alert mechanism is based on a simple yet effective comparison: the number of requests hitting our ALB, which represents the total log volume entering the system, versus the number of logs successfully archived in our long-term storage. By monitoring this ratio, we can ensure that what goes in must come out, providing a robust validation of our logging infrastructure's health. When the alert is triggered, it indicates a potential mismatch, prompting immediate investigation and remediation.

Sources indicate that in practice, this alert has proven to be a valuable tool, especially during periods of infrastructure refactoring. For instance, when we migrated our ALB to a VPC origin, the alert was instrumental in identifying and addressing the resulting log flow discrepancies. However, it has also saved us in less obvious scenarios. For example, when archive jobs failed to run due to unforeseen challenges, the alert flagged the missing archived logs, allowing us to promptly investigate and resolve the problem before it impacted our log analysis and retention processes.

Sources indicate that while this alert is a powerful tool, it is just one part of our comprehensive monitoring strategy. We continuously refine and adapt our logging infrastructure to handle the ever-increasing volume and complexity of log data. By combining proactive monitoring, efficient resource management, and a deep understanding of our system's behavior, Hugging Face ensures that our logging pipeline remains resilient, reliable, and capable of supporting our platform's growth and evolving needs. This alert is a testament to our commitment to maintaining a robust and transparent logging system, providing our teams with the insights they need to keep Hugging Face running smoothly.

According to recent reports, when operating cloud-native applications and Kubernetes-based infrastructures, even seemingly minor issues can escalate into significant downtime if left unchecked. This is particularly true for the Kubernetes API, which serves as the central nervous system of a Kubernetes cluster, orchestrating the creation, management, and networking of containers. At Hugging Face, we've learned through experience that monitoring the Kubernetes API error rate and rate limiting metrics is a crucial practice, one that can prevent potential disasters.

It has been revealed that hugging Face's infrastructure is deeply integrated with Kubernetes, and the kube-rs library has been instrumental in building and managing this ecosystem efficiently. kube-rs offers a Rust-centric approach to Kubernetes application development, providing developers with a familiar and powerful toolkit. At its core, kube-rs introduces three key concepts: reflectors, controllers, and custom resource interfaces. Reflectors ensure real-time synchronization of Kubernetes resources, enabling applications to react swiftly to changes. Controllers, the decision-makers, continuously reconcile the desired and actual states of resources, making Kubernetes self-healing. Custom resource interfaces extend Kubernetes, allowing developers to define application-specific resources for better abstraction.

Additionally, kube-rs introduces watchers and finalizers. Watchers monitor specific resources for changes, triggering actions in response to events. Finalizers, on the other hand, ensure proper cleanup and resource termination by defining custom logic. By providing Rust-based abstractions for these Kubernetes concepts, kube-rs allows developers to build robust, efficient applications, leveraging the Kubernetes platform's power and flexibility while maintaining a Rust-centric development approach. This integration streamlines the process of building and managing complex Kubernetes applications, making it a valuable tool in Hugging Face's infrastructure.

Hugging Face's integration with Kubernetes is a cornerstone of our infrastructure, and the kube-rs library plays a pivotal role in managing this ecosystem. The kube::api:: module is instrumental in automating various tasks, such as managing HTTPS certificates for custom domains supporting our Spaces product. By programmatically handling certificate lifecycles, we ensure the security and accessibility of our services, providing consumers with a seamless experience. Additionally, we have used this module outside of user-facing features during routine maintenance to facilitate node draining and termination providing cluster stability during infrastructure updates.

Sources indicate that the kube::runtime:: module has been equally crucial for us, enabling the development and deployment of custom controllers that enhance our infrastructure's automation and resilience. For instance, we've implemented controllers for billing management in our managed services, where watchers and finalizers on customer pods ensure accurate resource tracking and billing. This level of customization allows us to adapt Kubernetes to our specific needs.

It has been revealed that through kube-rs, Hugging Face has achieved a high level of efficiency, reliability, and control over our cloud-native applications. The library's Rust-centric design aligns with our engineering philosophy, allowing us to leverage Rust's strengths in managing Kubernetes resources. By automating critical tasks and building custom controllers, we've created a scalable, self-healing infrastructure that meets the diverse and evolving needs of our owners and enterprise customers. This integration demonstrates our commitment to harnessing the full potential of Kubernetes while maintaining a development approach tailored to our unique requirements.

In a recent development, while our infrastructure rarely encounters complications related to the Kubernetes API, we remain vigilant, especially during and after deployments. The Kubernetes API is a critical component in our use of kube::runtime:: for managing customer pods and cloud networking resources. Any disruptions or inefficiencies in API communication can have cascading effects on our services, potentially leading to downtime or degraded performance.

The importance of monitoring these API metrics is underscored by the experiences of other consumers of Kubernetes. OpenAI, for instance, shared a status update detailing how DNS availability challenges resulted in significant downtime. While not directly related to the Kubernetes API, their experience highlights the interconnectedness of various infrastructure components and the potential for cascading failures. Just as DNS availability is vital for application accessibility, a healthy and responsive Kubernetes API is essential for managing and orchestrating our containerized workloads.

Recent findings suggest that as a best practice, we've integrated these API metrics into our monitoring and alerting systems, ensuring that any anomalies or trends are promptly brought to our attention. This allows us to take a proactive approach, investigating and addressing problems before they impact our customers. For instance, on one occasion a single cluster started rate limiting requests to the Kubernetes API. We were able to trace this back to one of our third-party tools hitting a bug and repeatedly requesting a node be drained even though it had already done so. In response we were able to flush the malfunctioning job from the system before any noticeable degradation impacted our consumers. This is a great example that alerting scenarios do not just happen directly after deploying fresh versions of our custom controllers — bugs can take time to manifest as production issues.

Industry observers note that in conclusion, while our infrastructure is robust and well-architected, we recognize that vigilance and proactive monitoring are essential to maintaining its health and stability. By keeping a close eye on the Kubernetes API error rate and rate limiting metrics, we safeguard our managed services, ensure smooth customer experiences, and uphold our commitment to reliability and performance. This is a testament to our belief that in the world of cloud-native technologies, every component, no matter how small, plays a significant role in the overall resilience and success of our platform.

And a final bonus alert for reading through this far into the post!

According to recent reports, at Hugging Face, our experiments are constantly in flux, often with purpose-fit clusters spinning up and down as we iterate on features and products. To add to the entropy, our growth is also a significant factor, with clusters expanding to their limits and triggering meiosis-like splits to maintain balance. To navigate this dynamic environment without resorting to hardcoding or introducing an additional cluster discovery layer, we've devised a clever alert that adapts to these changes.

Recent findings suggest that the metric used in this query is container_network_transmit_packets_total, which represents the total number of packets transmitted by a container. The query is filtering for metrics from a cluster’s local Prometheus instance, which is tasked with metric collection as well as remote writing to our central metric store — Grafana Mimir. Transmission of packets approximates healthy remote writes, which is what we want to ensure across all active clusters.

According to recent reports, the first part of the query performs a current rate check. The second part of the query performs a historical rate check by using the same calculation as the current rate check plus an offset 48h clause. The -1 * multiplication is used to invert the result, so that if the historical rate is greater than 0, the result will be less than 0.

The or operator combines the two parts of the query. The query will return true if either of the following conditions is met:.

Industry observers note that the outer < 0 condition checks if the result of the or operation is less than 0. This means that the query will only trigger if neither of the conditions is met, i.e., if a cluster has never sent any metrics (both current and historical rates are 0).

There are two cases where the query will trigger:.

In both cases, the query will detect that the cluster is not sending any metrics and trigger the alert.

Sources indicate that this simple yet effective solution fires in scenarios where our metrics infrastructure crashes, during cluster setup, and when they're torn down providing us with timely insights into our infrastructure's health. While it may not be the most critical alert in our arsenal, it holds a special place since it was born out of collaboration. It is a testament to the power of teamwork through rigorous code review, made possible by the expertise and willingness to help of fellow colleagues in the Hugging Face infrastructure team 🤗.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It's impossible to have a massive game launch these days without some section of the internet, somewhere, finding grievances with the final product because it does not align with the expectations they had pre-release.

The most recent upset comes in the form of Grand Theft Auto 6's revised take on, well, grand theft auto. In case you're one of the few still unfamiliar, grand theft auto is more than the titular moniker for Rockstar's premier crime simulation series; it's actually a US legal term for the act of stealing or attempting to steal a motor vehicle. In most previous GTA entries, this was a central part of the core gameplay loop: accept a mission, nick a car, complete the mission, nick another car, getaway. It's an endemic part of the loop, and has become so popular and identifiable as such that even other games - Watch Dogs, Saint's Row, Cyberpunk 2077, and so on - have emulated the mechanic.

Recent findings suggest that so it makes sense that the internet is in a bit of a spin about GTA 6's more mature and restrained take on its eponymous crime. A quick, no-frills getaway in a vehicle you've hijacked on the road isn't always the most effective option. A mindless crime spree on the streets of Leonida is not a simple thing to pull off, nor an easy thing to live down. In this game, actions have consequences, and an ill-timed or ill-judged car jacking can swiftly and efficiently put an end to your criminal ambitions.

According to recent reports, that's not to say you cannot simply steal cars. Of course you can: the option to saunter up to an occupied vehicle and jack it from its registered owner is available to you from the very beginning of the game. But the citizens of Leonida aren't going to take your wanton act of foolishness lying down; many of the motorists in the county will fight back, pull a piece on you, or run you over mid-robbery attempt. Even if you are lucky to find one of the more pliant residents of the city, you might find something peculiar is happening in their car. I jacked a woman in the city over the weekend, and the cat she was ferrying from place to place decided to attack me, causing me to crash. I've heard other people say they've had muffled cries coming from the boot of the car where someone is transporting a hostage, or incidents where they've jacked the same person multiple times, leading to the poor car's owner to have a breakdown in the middle of the city.

That cat event, the team here at Eurogamer has worked out, is an early game trigger - it seems stealing random cars early in the game will increase the chance of this encounter occurring. Rockstar's guiding hand is more visible here, then, in trying to teach you a lesson: don't steal cars. You're given your own - Jason's two-door coupé utility, a Vapid Creado - that I actually formed quite an emotional bond with in the opening 10-or-so hours of the game. 'Look after this car,' Rockstar insists, tutorialising you how to repair it, customise it, make it all pretty so it's in good condition when you go pick up Lucia for the first time.

Shortly after the 10 hour marker, narrative events whisk you away elsewhere and you're given a 'slim jim', a long, thin tool that allows you to break into locked cars - something you could only do with a quick elbow jab before. The benefit here is two-fold; you can break into cars without setting off their alarms, and without breaking glass and lowering their resale value (something quite crucial in the earlier sections of the game). So, it takes you until Chapter 2 to start being able to more reliably and consistently break into vehicles. Good.

According to recent reports, and it'll take even longer to break into keyless vehicles. We're in 2026 after all, and it's heavily implied this is when GTA 6 is also set - it stands to reason that many cars run keyless fobs, and your old-school tools won't cut it if you want to break into a Zorruso, rather than an old Vapid truck. But then, even when you're well-armed and ready to start an illustrious new career as Vice City's most nefarious car thief, there's more to consider. Most modern cars also come with trackers: standard trackers simply prevent you modding cars you don't own (not an matter you'll face very often), but advanced trackers are more problematic.

Boosting a car with an advanced tracker immediately alerts the cops to your location, and they close in on you fast. The only answer to this problem is flooring it, and outspeeding the signal ping the tracker is sending out: you need to drive fast and cleanly in order to stay mobile long enough for the tracker to deactivate, and this often incurs damage that makes selling these cars to fences a less viable option. You can't even sell cars with trackers installed at all to some fences until you're much, much further into the game.

According to recent reports, so, long story short, stealing cars is a faff in GTA 6. But I like that. I like that Rockstar has evolved the gameplay formula to more accurately reflect the state of the world in 2026. Modern problems require modern answers, and given that Rockstar has gone above and beyond in its creation of a sandbox simulation of Florida, I feel the immersion would be broken by just being able to saunter up to any car you want and break into it. No, needing a 'slim jim' or a key cloner - or needing to case my victims properly before trying to jack them - makes for a better game as far as I'm concerned. It makes me roleplay Jason and Lucia better, it makes me engage with the game's systems more, it makes me appreciate the cars that I do have whilst I have them.

It also improves the flow of the game and how I interact with missions. I recently played GTA: Vice City, and after most missions were wrapped up, I would simply fling the nearest motorist onto the sidewalk, hop in their car, and drive away into the Malibu-styled sunset. I can't simply do that in GTA 6: I need to think about my getaway options, whether there's heat on my car, and where my next best (and cheapest) ride is going to be if a robbery or raid goes awry. 'Ah,' I think, 'I understand why there's a garage next to that safehouse on the map now.'.

In making the act of grand theft auto harder and more awkward, Rockstar has nudged me into playing Grand Theft Auto the game like a more thoughtful criminal. I play it like someone on the run, who wouldn't just be indiscriminately committing wanton acts of felony theft on a whim, just because I didn't want to run four blocks down the road to meet my pals for a drink. It's a gorgeous example of functionality, design, and narrative dovetailing - one of the key reasons this is a five star game. The complaints about the system, to my ear, don't reflect what Rockstar has built here. Plus, if it bothers you that much, you could always try to play GTA 6 like a mindless thug if you really want to - just expect the world to treat you like one, too.

#218364. Power BI MCP server: how to brief an AI agent to build accurate measures

Power BI MCP server: how to brief an AI agent to build accurate measures

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (3074 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sitepoint

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.
  • Industry observers note that power BI, Microsoft's reporting and dashboard tool, now lets an AI agent work on the data model behind a report.
  • Recent findings suggest that the agent did a careful job, but its formula didn't follow the same rules the finance team uses to count revenue.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that power BI, Microsoft's reporting and dashboard tool, now lets an AI agent work on the data model behind a report. If you ask one to add a year-on-year revenue measure (a measure is Power BI's name for a saved calculation) with Microsoft's MCP server connected, it can write the formula and save it to the model without you opening the formula bar. When we tried this on a sample model, an agent inspected the model, wrote the measure, tested it and saved it in under four minutes.

Recent findings suggest that the agent did a careful job, but its formula didn't follow the same rules the finance team uses to count revenue. Nobody had told it what "revenue" meant in this business, so it had to decide for itself. We then gave another agent a short brief that set out finance's rules for what counts as revenue and which date to count it by. The agent wrote the formula from those rules, and the result matched finance's figure exactly. The two results show how much difference it makes in how you brief an AI agent to build accurate measures.

Industry observers note that we wanted to find out what an agent can see in a Power BI model and how to brief it so the measure matches the business's own definitions, with the setup arranged so that every change can be checked. Developers will know the principle from agents that write SQL or API code, where the brief ends up doing the job of a specification.

Because MCP (Model Context Protocol) is an open standard, the same server can be used from different AI clients, GitHub Copilot in VS Code and Claude among them, although some clients need extra sign-in setup for the hosted version.

Power BI has two current MCP servers, plus an older one, the Power BI Consumption MCP server, kept for existing integrations. The first of the current pair is the Power BI Authoring MCP server, which you may still see under the name of its package, powerbi-modeling-mcp. It lets an agent create and change the objects inside a semantic model, which is the layer of a Power BI report that holds the tables, the relationships between them and the calculations, kept separate from the charts on the page. It comes in two forms. The hosted version, still in preview, needs nothing installed. The local version is generally available and runs on your own machine, which makes it the one to use when the model is a file you hold yourself, whether that's open in Power BI Desktop, the free Windows app used to build reports, or saved as a project folder. Macs aren't supported by the local version, so on a Mac it has to be the hosted one, which works only with models published to Microsoft's cloud (a Fabric workspace).

The second is the Fabric IQ MCP server. Fabric IQ is part of Microsoft Fabric, the wider data platform that Power BI now sits within. It gives an agent read-only tools for finding published reports and models and running queries against them, within the permissions already set, so the agent can answer questions about the data but can't change a model.

In a recent development, which one to use follows from the job. Anything that changes a model goes through the authoring server, whether that's a new measure, a relationship or a set of descriptions, and it has to be the local version if the model is a Desktop file or a project folder under source control. Fabric IQ is for agents that only need answers from models other people maintain.

In a recent development, an agent connected to a semantic model can see its metadata (table and column names, data types, relationships, existing measures and any descriptions someone has written) and can run queries against the data. Everything it produces is inferred from those clues. A model that has served a business for years carries names that made perfect sense to the people who built it, and a column called Amt on a table called Sales_v2 tells an agent far less than it tells them.

Recent findings suggest that names carry a lot of the meaning. A column called Amount could hold the value with VAT (the UK's sales tax) or without, before credit notes or after, and an agent asked for "revenue" has to pick one. If the model holds several revenue measures built for different reports, the agent has to choose between them, and the one it picks may have been built for a different purpose.

In a recent development, the formulas depend on context as well. Power BI measures use a syntax of their own called DAX, which stands for Data Analysis Expressions. A DAX result shifts with whatever the person viewing the report has filtered or clicked on, which is known as filter context. A developer might think of a measure as a function that reads implicit state set by its caller. The same measure can be right as a single total on a card and need different handling once it's split by product in a table or filtered by a date slicer (the on-page date filter), depending on how CALCULATE (the DAX function that changes which filters apply) is used. Which behaviour is correct depends on how the business wants the number to respond, and that's something the agent has to be told.

In a recent development, relationships work the same way. Plenty of models have more than one date column on the sales table, say order date and dispatch date, with only one relationship active at a time. A DAX measure uses the active relationship unless it's written to switch to the other one, and the agent has no way of knowing which date your monthly reporting runs on unless something tells it.

In a recent development, in each case the agent can write a valid measure. Which of two valid measures matches the business's own definition is the part it can't see from the model.

To see this in practice, we built a small sales model in a Power BI Desktop file, working through the server itself, with invented data: 5,266 order lines, with order dates from January 2025 to October 2026. We gave the Sales table an Amt column holding each line's value after discount with 20% VAT added, next to LineTotal and Discount columns that excluded VAT, and an existing [Revenue] measure that summed Amt. There were two date columns, with the active relationship to the Date table on dispatch date and the order date relationship inactive. Orders stop at the end of October 2026, which made the current year a part year, a deliberate test. Nothing in the model had a description. In this made-up business, finance reports revenue net of VAT and discounts, by order date.

Sources indicate that on 12 November 2026 we connected an AI agent (Anthropic's Claude Fable 5.2) to version 1.0.1 of the local server through a small Node.js script that speaks MCP over stdio. In all three runs the agent had the server's tools only, without Microsoft's powerbi-authoring plugin, which adds modelling guidance on top of them. It was also told that nobody was available to answer questions, so each measure was saved exactly as the agent wrote it, with no review in between. The first prompt was one sentence: "Add a year-on-year revenue measure.".

Recent findings suggest that before writing anything, the agent listed the tables, relationships and columns, read the existing measure, sampled some rows and checked the date ranges. It worked out for itself that 2026 was a part year and limited the comparison to the same dates in 2025, which avoided a misleading result of -6.7%. From 15 sample rows it also spotted that Amt looked like the net figure plus 20%.

The measure it saved reused the existing [Revenue] measure and followed the active relationship. This is the core of it, with the date handling and blank checks left out. CurrentDates is defined in those lines as the dates up to the last order:.

It returned growth of 21.5% for 2026, which is correct for revenue counted by dispatch date. On finance's definition, by order date, the answer is 18.6%, and the whole difference came from that choice of date. The VAT question made no difference to a percentage, because Amt was already net of discount and every line carried the same rate, although it would have overstated any figure in pounds by 20%.

We reset the model and repeated the run with a fresh agent, which made the same two choices and returned the same 21.5%. Both choices were reasonable readings of the model as it stood, and the DAX was sound. In their reports, both agents flagged the date basis and the VAT treatment as open questions, and both worked out that an order-date basis would give 18.6%. That's what a good analyst would do, and with those two answers they would have had everything they needed.

It has been revealed that think of a capable analyst on their first morning, someone who knows DAX well but has never seen your business before and knows nothing (or not a lot) about it. You wouldn't say "add a revenue measure" and walk off. You'd tell them which table holds the trusted figures, whether revenue includes VAT, which date drives the reporting calendar, and what they shouldn't touch. An agent needs that briefing for the same reasons, and getting good work out of it draws on the skills you'd use with any new starter. Developers do the same thing when they write a good ticket. A request for a measure is a requirement, and it needs the same definitions and constraints, plus a way to check the result.

Sources indicate that before you send a prompt, ask yourself whether you could do the task properly if you were given only the words in that prompt and the model itself. If the answer is no, then the agent is in the same position, and it will make its own assumptions.

For the detailed run we cleared the earlier measure from the model and gave a fresh agent this brief:.

It has been revealed that this time the measure summed LineTotal minus Discount and used USERELATIONSHIP, the DAX function that switches a calculation to an inactive relationship, to work from order date. It returned 18.6% from that one brief, with no follow-up prompt, which is the figure we had calculated separately from the source data. This is the full measure as the agent saved it:.

Each line of the brief answered a question the agent would otherwise have had to settle alone. It also made some sensible decisions the brief hadn't covered. It left the grand total blank, for instance, where a plain total across both years would have shown a meaningless growth figure of 151.2%. The final line of the brief, asking to see the DAX before anything is saved, is there so that a person can see choices like that. In the test we approved that step in advance, to keep the run unattended.

Recent findings suggest that one detail needs adjusting before this measure is reused on other data. Its guard checks that each comparison period starts on or after the first order date, which works here because the sample data has an order on 1 January 2025. When we swapped that date for 2 January 2025 in a copy of the measure, January 2026 and the 2026 row came back blank. Comparing against the first date in the Date table, as the first agent's measure did, brought the 2026 figure back, since the Date table starts on 1 January. That version doesn't confirm that sales exist for the whole comparison period, though, so the right check depends on whether the business wants growth shown only where a complete prior period exists. That's a decision for whoever reviews the measure.

We ran the one-sentence prompt twice and the detailed brief once, all with the same AI model and one small set of data, which is enough to illustrate the pattern but too little to say how often it happens.

Good briefs help, but you'll be writing the same definitions into prompts again and again unless they live in the model itself. Descriptions on tables, columns and measures are part of the metadata the agent reads, so filling them in is one of the cheapest ways to put business definitions in front of it every time. In our test, where nothing had a description, both agents given the one-sentence prompt noted that nothing confirmed what Amt contained. A description such as "Net sales value in GBP, excluding VAT, after credit notes" stays in the model, where the agent reads it without anyone retyping it.

Industry observers note that naming deserves the same attention. Spelling out abbreviated column names, hiding technical keys that no report needs, gathering measures into a single measures table, and removing measures that are no longer used all give the agent fewer things to choose between. These are the same habits that make a model easier for a newly introduced colleague to pick up, so asking someone outside the team to find a figure in it is a fair test of the result.

In a recent development, microsoft has also added a set of Prep data for AI features (in preview) to Power BI Desktop and the service. They let you choose which fields Copilot, Microsoft's AI assistant, should consider and write AI instructions that explain your business terms, with verified answers available for common questions. They're aimed at Copilot, but deciding and writing down your definitions is the same work whichever AI tool reads them.

An agent working through the authoring server has the same access as the person signed in, so anything that person can change, the agent can change. Sign in with an account that has no more access than the job needs, and take a copy of the model first, as you would before any bulk edit.

Recent findings suggest that start with read-only mode. The local server takes a --readonly flag that blocks all write operations, which is the right setting while you're learning how the agent behaves on your models. When we tried to create a measure in this mode, the server refused and mentioned it was running read-only. In VS Code, the configuration looks like this (other clients use a similar structure, sometimes under an mcpServers key instead of servers):.

You'll need Node.js installed for the npx command. The server won't run other tools until its licence terms (the EULA) have been accepted. Once you've read them, you can either tell the agent to accept for you or add --accepteula to the args list.

Industry observers note that the --readonly flag belongs to the local server. On a Mac the route is the hosted server and a copy of the model in a Fabric workspace, once a Fabric administrator has switched on the tenant setting that allows the MCP endpoint, and there the copy is the safeguard. For an enforced limit, sign in with an account that holds only Build permission on the model, which lets the agent read and query it and nothing more.

Industry observers note that read-write is the default, so check how confirmation behaves in the version you install. Version 1.0.1 skips confirmation prompts by default, which the project's README hasn't caught up with, and has a --require-confirmation flag to turn them on. The flag is listed in the server's own --help output. In our runs every edit went through without a prompt. When we added the flag to the args list, the server asked for confirmation before the first write, with a message beginning "Are you sure you want to perform operations that will modify your database", and answering no blocked the change.

Recent findings suggest that version control is the other safeguard. Saved in the Power BI Project format (PBIP), a report and its model become folders of text files instead of one binary .pbix file. Commit those before the agent starts and its work arrives as an ordinary diff, which you can review and revert like any other change.

It has been revealed that whatever the agent reads, including table and column names and the rows returned by any query, is passed on to the AI provider behind your client, which may sit outside Microsoft's compliance commitments. For a model holding customer or payroll data, check that the provider is approved under your data policies before you connect.

In a recent development, an agent can draft and test a measure in minutes, and someone still has to read what comes back. For a developer fresh to Power BI, that takes enough DAX to see what a measure's filters will do in a table broken down by month or product, and enough knowledge of the business to confirm the agent used the right column and the right date. Writing the brief takes the same knowledge. Ours could only have come from someone who knew the model had an inactive relationship and which columns carried VAT.

These are data modelling and DAX skills, which many learners find the hardest part of Power BI. If the person reviewing agent output hasn't had that grounding yet, it helps to know how to judge whether a Power BI course covers enough DAX and data modelling, because courses vary a great deal in how much time they give to those two subjects compared with building charts.

In a recent development, take a copy of a model you know well and connect the local server to it in read-only mode. Ask the agent to describe every table and measure in its own words, then check those descriptions against what you know the model does. Wherever the two differ, the model needs a clearer name or a written description, and the corrected text can go straight into the description fields. With those in place before you allow any writes, the agent starts its first real task with the same definitions your finance team uses.

A football referee has denied accusations of being drunk after being removed from a match at halftime following a bizarre incident in which he showed a yellow card to a goalkeeper nearly half the pitch away from a foul.

Syrian referee Hanna Hattab was officiating an AFC Champions League Two match between the United Arab Emirates’ Al Jazira and Iran’s Gol Gohar when his decision-making raised eyebrows.

In the 32nd minute, Hattab awarded a free kick following a foul by Al Jazira’s Felicio Milson and approached the winger with a yellow card in hand.

However, as reported by the Daily Mail, the referee appeared to receive a message through his earpiece before suddenly changing direction and walking toward Al Jazira goalkeeper Ersin Destanoglu.

Despite being nowhere near the foul, the stunned goalkeeper was shown a yellow card.

Hattab eventually overturned the decision after consulting his fourth official, while Milson avoided receiving what would have been his second yellow card of the match.

Gol Gohar manager Mehdi Rahmati was reportedly seen shouting “he’s drunk” at Hattab, while the club’s sporting director, Heydar Afsari, revealed the team had threatened to boycott the second half.

“The referee against Al Jazira was not in a normal state, and even Al Jazira’s players told us the same thing,” Afsari mentioned.

It has been revealed that 🚨| WATCH: A referee was allegedly DRUNK during an AFC Champions League II match and had to be replaced at half-time. 😳Fans say he looked completely LOST and even booked a goalkeeper for a foul in midfield. Players from both teams say they saw him drinking before kick-off. 😬….

Hattab was ultimately replaced by the fourth official at halftime, with Al Jazira winning 1-0 thanks to a goal from Anderson Talisca.

However, the referee has since denied the allegations and threatened legal action against those responsible for spreading them.

According to BBC Sport, Omani sports journalist Issa Said claimed there was a medical explanation for Hattab’s unusual behavior.
